quickAnswer: A 2,000 sq ft suite typically pays $0.14-$0.24 per sq ft per encapsulation event, and frequently just the $175-$300 vendor minimum, while 25,000+ sq ft floors pay about $0.05-$0.10. Because encapsulation production is so fast, mobilization and minimums make up most of a small job's cost, so small tenants save the most by bundling with routine janitorial visits or neighboring suites.

blocks.text: Why encapsulation scale effects are sharper than extraction

Encapsulation is fast. A trained technician with an orbital machine can treat 1,500-3,000 sq ft per hour depending on layout. That speed means the actual cleaning on a 2,000 sq ft suite takes barely an hour, while drive time, loading, pre-vacuuming setup, and paperwork take nearly as long. On a 30,000 sq ft floor, the same fixed overhead is a sliver of a full night's production. The result is a price curve that drops more steeply than hot-water extraction across the size brackets.

Minimum charges amplify the curve. Most standalone encapsulation vendors set minimums of $175-$300 per visit. Any suite under roughly 1,500 sq ft is effectively paying a flat fee, regardless of the posted unit rate.
Benchmark rates from small suites to large floors

blocks.title: Scale gap: about 3x from smallest to largest
blocks.text: Effective encapsulation cost per sq ft falls from roughly $0.20 at 1,200 sq ft to about $0.07 at 40,000 sq ft, nearly a threefold drop. Hot-water extraction shows a similar but slightly flatter curve because large extraction jobs still carry hose runs, drying, and truck-mount operating costs.
Worked example: the same crew, two buildings

Take a vendor billing technician time at $70 per hour with about $120 in fixed mobilization per visit and chemicals near $0.015 per sq ft. In a 2,000 sq ft architecture studio with two private offices, one technician working at 1,600 sq ft per hour finishes in 1.25 hours. Labor is about $88, mobilization $120, chemicals $30, for a cost near $238. With margin, the quote lands around $300, or $0.15 per sq ft, right at the low end of the small-office bracket.

On a 30,000 sq ft open-plan insurance floor, two technicians at 2,700 sq ft per hour each finish in about 5.6 hours. Labor is roughly $784, mobilization still around $120, chemicals $450, for a total near $1,354, or $0.045 per sq ft. With margin, the quote comes in around $0.06 per sq ft. Labor per square foot dropped by about 40%, but mobilization per square foot dropped by more than 90%, which is where most of the scale advantage lives.
How small offices narrow the gap

items.name: Add encapsulation to the nightly janitorial visit
items.text: If your cleaner already visits, the mobilization is already paid for. Ask for encapsulation priced as a per-sq-ft add-on with no separate minimum.

items.name: Coordinate with neighbors
items.text: Two or three small tenants on one floor booking the same night can each pay close to the mid-size bracket rate.

items.name: Encapsulate lanes on a tighter cycle
items.text: Treat 600-900 sq ft of entry and corridor carpet monthly rather than the entire suite quarterly. You stay near the minimum but get far better appearance.

items.name: Prepare the floor
items.text: Clear chair mats, bins, and under-desk storage before the visit so the technician spends the full hour on carpet.

items.name: Sign a 12-month program
items.text: Recurring bookings let the vendor route your suite with nearby jobs, which is often enough to waive the minimum.

items: Measured carpeted area, not gross rentable area, is used for pricing.
Production assumptions are stated, so a $0.06 rate is not quietly delivered as a single fast pass with no pre-vacuum.
Nightly vacuuming is in the janitorial scope to remove encapsulated crystals; otherwise soil stays in the carpet.
At least one annual hot-water extraction is scheduled to satisfy carpet warranty requirements and flush residue.
Elevator lobbies and entries are flagged for more frequent treatment than interior office zones.

blocks.text: Supporting tools for in-house daily care

Encapsulation pays off longest where daily soil control is strong. Small offices often keep a non-electric 9.5-inch carpet sweeper with dual debris bins at roughly 4.5 lb for quick daytime pickup in reception areas, which avoids running a vacuum during client meetings. Large-floor janitorial teams running mixed carpet and hard floors should keep mop water away from carpet edges: a 35-quart splash-reducing bucket with a side-press wringer limits drips at transitions, and a 20-pad microfiber charging bucket with a snap lid and color-coded pads keeps restroom pads from ever touching break-room or corridor floors. Clean hard-floor transitions mean less sticky residue migrating onto carpet and attracting soil between encapsulation visits.

blocks.title: Documentation applies at every size
blocks.text: Small or large, require a certificate of insurance naming you and your landlord, Safety Data Sheets for the encapsulant and spotters under OSHA Hazard Communication rules, and Green Seal or Safer Choice chemistry where occupants are sensitive. Small one-person vendors are the most likely to lack current documentation.

faqs.q: At what square footage do encapsulation minimums stop mattering?
faqs.a: For most vendors, around 1,500-2,000 sq ft. Below that, the posted per-sq-ft rate times your area falls below the $175-$300 minimum and you pay the flat fee. Above it, the unit rate drives the invoice. Bundling with routine janitorial service is the most reliable way for very small suites to avoid the minimum.

faqs.q: Is encapsulation better suited to small or large offices?
faqs.a: It works well at both scales, but the value proposition differs. Large floors benefit from extremely low unit pricing and same-night drying across tens of thousands of square feet. Small offices benefit from minimal disruption and fast turnaround, even if the effective price per sq ft is higher. Both still need periodic hot-water extraction.

faqs.q: How should I budget a monthly encapsulation program?
faqs.a: Multiply carpeted area by rate and events per year, then divide by 12. A 2,000 sq ft office at the $300 minimum encapsulated bimonthly costs $1,800 per year, or $150 per month. Dividing by 4.333 weeks per month gives about $35 per week, which you can compare against your weekly janitorial invoice.

faqs.q: Do large-floor vendors need different insurance than small ones?
faqs.a: The coverage types are the same: general liability, workers compensation, and often auto liability, with your company and landlord named as additional insureds. Large buildings frequently require higher limits, such as $2 million per occurrence or umbrella coverage, set in the lease or building contractor rules. Verify limits before the first service night.

faqs.q: Can I mix encapsulation in small zones with extraction on the rest of a large floor?
faqs.a: Yes, and many facility managers do. Encapsulate high-traffic lanes, entries, and break areas monthly while scheduling hot-water extraction of the whole floor once or twice a year. Ask vendors to price each zone separately so you can see how the size bracket affects each portion of the program.
